deep.reconstruction:
This page is page (2) of Ramanujan's manuscript of his paper 'On the integral ∫_0^x tan^{-1}t/t dt' (J. Indian Math. Soc. 7 (1915); Collected Papers no. 11). Here Φ(x)=∫_0^x arctan(t)/t dt = x − x^3/3^2 + x^5/5^2 − …, the inverse tangent integral Ti_2(x), and Φ(1)=G is Catalan's constant. The next page computes Φ(1)=0.9159655942.

(8) Write t=tan x, s=sin x, c=cos x. Since Σ r^n sin(nθ)/n^2 = Im Li_2(r e^{iθ}), the left side is
L(α) = Im Li_2((1−1/α) c e^{ix}) + Im Li_2((1−α) s · i e^{ix}).
The claim is L(α) = Φ(t) − Φ(αt) + x log α.
Verification (mine), by differentiating in α:
- d/dα Li_2(z) = −log(1−z)/z · z'.
- First term: 1 − z1 = (αs^2 + c^2 − i(α−1)sc)/α. Its derivative contributes A/(α(α−1)), where A = arctan((α−1)sc/(c^2+αs^2)).
- Second term: 1 − z2 = c^2 + αs^2 + i(α−1)sc. It contributes −A/(α−1).
- So L'(α) = −A/α.
- The right side has derivative (x − arctan(αt))/α.
- These agree because tan(arctan(αt) − x) = (α−1)t/(1+αt^2) = (α−1)sc/(c^2+αs^2) = tan A.
- Both sides vanish at α=1, so (8) holds where the series converge (α>0, suitable x).

(9) For |x|<1: Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k (2k+1) log(1 − x^2/(2k+1)^2) = (4/π)[Φ(1) − Φ(tan(π(1−x)/4))] + log tan(π(1−x)/4).
Verification (mine):
- Use (π/4) sec(πx/2) = Σ (−1)^k (2k+1)/((2k+1)^2 − x^2). The derivative of the left side is −(πx/2) sec(πx/2).
- On the right, put u = tan(π(1−x)/4) and use Φ'(u) = arctan(u)/u. The derivative is [π(1−x)/2 − π/2]/cos(πx/2), the same thing.
- Both sides are 0 at x=0.

(10) Put x=2/3 in (9) and exponentiate. Then tan(π/12) = 2−√3, and the needed value is Φ(2−√3) = (2/3)G + (π/12) log(2−√3); this is the standard evaluation, stated rather than derived here. The right side becomes 4G/(3π) − (2/3) log(2+√3), giving
Π (1 − 4/(3(2k+1))^2)^{(−1)^k(2k+1)} = e^{4G/(3π)}/(2+√3)^{2/3}.

(11) This is (9) with x → ix, valid for real x: Σ (−1)^k (2k+1) log(1 + x^2/(2k+1)^2) = (4/π)[Φ(1) − Φ(e^{−πx/2})] − 2x arctan(e^{−πx/2}).
Verification (mine): both sides have derivative (πx/2) sech(πx/2). Here 2v/(1+v^2) = sech(πx/2) with v = e^{−πx/2}. Both sides vanish at x=0.

(12) Put x = (2/π) log(2+√3) in (11), so e^{−πx/2} = 2−√3 and arctan(2−√3) = π/12. The log terms cancel and the right side is 4G/(3π):
Π (1 + {2 log(2+√3)/((2k+1)π)}^2)^{(−1)^k(2k+1)} = e^{4G/(3π)}.

(13) Take |β|<1 and πα/2 = log tan(π(1+β)/4). Then e^{−πα/2} = tan(π(1−β)/4), so the Φ-terms of (11) at α and (9) at β coincide. Subtracting (9) from (11) gives
−2α · π(1−β)/4 + πα/2 = παβ/2.
Hence Π_k ((n^2+α^2)/(n^2−β^2))^{(−1)^k n} = e^{παβ/2}, with n = 2k+1.
errors: No mathematical errors found; all of (8)–(13) check out (derivative checks of (8), (9), (11) and the special values in (10), (12), (13)).
Minor: the conditions for (8) (α>0 and convergence of both series, e.g. |(1−1/α)cos x|<1 and |(1−α)sin x|<1) are not stated on this page.
(10) and (12) use the value Φ(2−√3) = (2/3)Φ(1) + (π/12)log(2−√3) without proof on this page (presumably established on page (1)).

results.modern_name: Functional relation for the inverse tangent integral Ti_2 (imaginary parts of Li_2)
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan, J. Indian Math. Soc. 7 (1915); see also Lewin, Polylogarithms

results.modern_name: Inverse tangent integral evaluations of log-sine/secant-type series
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan (1915 paper; Notebooks, Berndt Part I ch. 2)

results.modern_name: Elementary consequence (Gudermannian-type relation between α and β)
